claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a simple, single-phase solid solution.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi solid solution has relatively uniform atomic spacing and low lattice distortion.
The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by a scarcity of intrinsic obstacles to dislocation motion.
The starting alloy has limited lattice distortion and lacks nanoscale precipitates and short-range order.
Low intrinsic obstacle density permits easy dislocation glide in CoCrFeNiTi.
Dislocations in the alloy undergo dynamic recovery through annihilation or rearrangement.
Easy glide and dynamic recovery lower work hardening, hardness, and strength while retaining high plasticity and machinability.
Atomic-size differences and localized lattice distortions in nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are insufficient to pin dislocations strongly.
Compression or tension testing and microstructural characterization can be used to examine low-temperature deformation mechanisms in a multicomponent solid-solution alloy.
Moderate cold work followed by annealing can be used to create precipitates or refined grains in CoCrFeNiTi.
Room-temperature and cryogenic or moderately low-temperature mechanical testing is an applicable loading regime for the proposed comparison.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to quasi-static loading of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi that initially contains no secondary phases.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit low yield strength and hardness together with a high capacity for plastic deformation.
Deformed starting-state material will contain a high density of mobile dislocations with little evidence of strong pinning by clusters or precipitates.
Samples processed to contain precipitates or refined grains will exhibit stronger dislocation pinning than the starting material.
Introducing microstructural obstacles will appreciably increase the hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
Single-phase, equal- or near-equal-concentration HEAs can combine substantial strength with plastic deformation or ductility.
The quantitative contributions of lattice friction and dynamic recovery to CoCrFeNiTi strength have not been directly measured.
Evidence of strong dislocation pinning in the starting state, or failure of verified induced obstacles to increase strength and hardness, would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
